baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Egypt and historical consciousness in Diop’s reconstruction of African history (1954–1981)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Tine’s section 2 and the publisher’s account establish Diop’s effort to restore African historical agency by placing ancient Egypt within African history. His diffusionist explanations are his contested theses, not accepted facts about a homogeneous continent.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Egypt and historical consciousness in Diop’s reconstruction of African history (1954–1981)

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Historical and cultural continuity as a basis for Pan-African independence and federation (1960–1981)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Tine distinguishes Diop’s historical-cultural project from Senghor’s négritude while connecting both with anticolonial politics. The 1960 platform is dated by the publisher; no common doctrine or direct influence on other named historians is inferred.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Historical and cultural continuity as a basis for Pan-African independence and federation (1960–1981)

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Amady Aly Dieng contests Diop’s account of national identity and cultural borrowing (1989–1995), as Tine reports
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Tine’s section 2 attributes to Dieng objections that Diop privileged race in explaining nationhood and insufficiently distinguished cultural creation from selective borrowing. The originals are unread; this named mediated critique is routed through African historiography, not asserted as its collective verdict.
